La Converse va à la rencontre de Raccoon: La Converse meets Raccoon at Studio Forge for an enriching conversation about the rapper’s identity
Raccoon dans le studio d'enregistrement: Raccoon in the K-Status recording studio. Photo: Ahmed El Moudden
Avec un parcours jalonné d’obstacles et: With a path marked by obstacles and challenges, Raccoon has skillfully turned his experiences into a source of inspiration for his young audience. On a Saturday night, close to Crémazie station, La Converse meets Raccoon at Studio Forge to begin an enriching conversation about the rapper’s identity and how it drives him to contribute to the life of his community.
Après sa séance d’enregistrement, l’arti: After his recording session, the artist invites us into the studio, where a purple haze envelops us. A deep, pulsing beat fills the room, carrying us into the world of hip-hop. With lyrics like “<l1>You can be dope, even if you have nothing to sell</l1>,” the rapper tells young people they can be respected, like “real guys from the hood,” while staying within the law and without falling into delinquency. The artist redefines success and urges listeners not to rely on social conventions and to look for their own path. “I embody success by being a young Black man from the neighbourhoods who makes a living from his lyricism,” he tells us.
Racoon, de son vrai nom, Shamyr Daléus-L: Raccoon, whose real name is Shamyr Daléus-Louis, grew up in the northeast of the city, between the neighbourhoods of Montréal-Nord, Rivière-des-Prairies and Pointe-aux-Trembles. His passion for music and words was nurtured from his earliest childhood. “I fell into music because I come from a deeply musical family. My big brother raps, and my sister brought us the best sounds from the United States. We’ve been big fans of American hip-hop culture for as long as I can remember.” Little by little, French rap caught the young artist’s interest. “I really started getting into rap when I discovered the conscious rap of <l1>Kery James</l1> and <l2>Youssoupha</l2>,” he says.
À l’âge de 15 ans, Shamyr s’est procuré: At 15, Shamyr got his hands on Youssoupha’s album Noir Désir, a work that left a deep mark on him. “It’s the first album I bought with my own allowance, and I was very attached to it,” he says. “In his interviews, Youssoupha quoted authors like Frantz Fanon. Authors, and concepts, that my father had talked to me about before. The album dealt with subjects like Black consciousness, Black history, the journey of the Black man, and all of that was at the centre of his creative process. I drew inspiration from his struggles and from the way he wrote and thought about rap. I was also raised on hip-hop that way. Later on, I got into Quebec rap.”
« Entendre des rappeurs français citer d: “Hearing French rappers quote writers my father had made me read when I was young created bonds with my parents. I love writing, and my parents are very literary, so it was a way of introducing them to rap through conscious rap,” adds the rapper.
« Mes deux parents sont quand même très: “Both my parents are really well integrated here,” he says, referring to their arrival from Haiti at a young age. “They showed me the culture here, and the culture of my country of origin too. Above all, they showed me how to move around here, in Quebec. They prepared me for the white man, but at the same time, they also taught me to love the place where I am and to make it my own, telling me, ‘You have a right to your place; we didn’t pay taxes for nothing,’” Shamyr explains about his upbringing.
C’est donc en se fondant sur son enfance: So it was drawing on his childhood and upbringing, thanks to his interest in literature and a few writing workshops he attended in his public housing complex (HLM) and in extracurricular programs, that Raccoon began to forge his artistic identity.
Le nom de scène de Shamyr, Raccoon, est: Shamyr’s stage name, Raccoon, is tied to habits from his teenage years, marked by a lack of sleep. “It goes back to my high school years. When I got to school, I had huge dark circles under my eyes. So my friends would say, ‘Figui raccoon,’ you’ve got a raccoon face. It was because of my interest in writing, since I spent nights writing, but also playing video games like Resident Evil, which has a fictional city, Raccoon City. So it’s a link between all those worlds,” explains the rapper, who was once known as Raccity, again in reference to Resident Evil and his sleepless nights.
Aujourd’hui âgé de 26 ans, Raccoon nous: Now 26, Raccoon tells us this stage name still represents his rebellious soul just as well. “It’s seen as harmless, but it can do whatever it wants. It’s one of the only animals whose intelligence hasn’t been put to the service of man,” he adds with a half-smile.
« Le but, c’est de faire bouger les espr: “The goal is to move minds and heads before behinds”
Si plusieurs rappeurs Montréalais se spé: While many Montréal rappers specialize in street rap, where women, guns and money fill their writing, Raccoon instead questions society, its values, its injustices. “Conscious rap is rap that wants to make demands, with a message to get across. Its purpose is to convince, or to open up a debate, ask a question, push people to think,” the artist explains. Borrowing the words of Kery James, he goes deeper: “The goal is to move minds and heads before behinds.”
Le Montréalais aborde la dure réalité de: The Montréal native tackles the harsh reality of neighbourhoods affected by gun violence. “These days it’s shoot shoot, bang bang / Can’t walk in the wing no more,” he chants in one of his songs. “When street rappers sing about shooting people, they still dance. Shoot is Raccoon’s perspective, from the other side of the barrel. We dance too,” he explains, commenting on the choreography that goes with the chorus, symbolic of his community’s resilience.
Raccoon en train d’enregistrer une chans: Raccoon recording a song in the K-Status recording studio. Photo: Ahmed El Moudden
Pour l’immigrant de deuxième génération,: For the second-generation immigrant, the question of identity is central. The artist takes it on in his latest album, titled C00N: La prophétie. “I’ve been told I use too many syllables, that I rap like a white guy,” says Raccoon, referring to the lyrics of his song C00N.
Il explique que le terme « C00N », qui d: He explains that the term “C00N,” which gives the song and the album their title, “is the N-word that Black people use for other Black people to say they act like white people, that they’re white people pleasers.” Historically, <l1>the term</l1>, which comes from the English word for raccoon, was used by white people as a slur for Black people. The word was later used by Black people to refer to an intruder in their midst.
« Dans les groupes de jeunes, quand un j: “In youth groups, when a young Black man or a young Black woman starts to ‘speak well,’ they’re stripped of their identity, and the person becomes ‘white,’” Shamyr elaborates. This reality saddens him. “I’d like us to get rid of that kind of label, the idea that what I do is meant for white people because I have a slightly more polished writing style… We have a hard time loving ourselves, appreciating ourselves for anything other than negativity,” laments the Montréal-Nord native.
En abordant cette question, le rappeur e: In addressing this issue, the conscious rapper insists that “excellence doesn’t belong to whiteness.” “Excellence belongs to us,” he stresses, hand on heart. “We’ve had great orators. We’ve had lyricists. Lyricism in rap comes from Black culture at its roots.” For him, his album is a campaign to convince the community to walk with him.
« Tout comme je veux critiquer les membr: “Just as I want to criticize members of my community for the boxes we try to fit ourselves into, it’s also important for me to remind them that I love them, that I come from the same place and that we share a common bond,” he says. His new collaborator Jackson adds that Raccoon’s song Mon Flag, made in collaboration with rapper Izzy-S, has resonated with many young Haitians.
Pendant plus d’un an, Raccoon a travaill: For more than a year, Raccoon worked as a youth worker at a youth centre. The experience was a revelation for him when it came to mental health. “At first, I wanted to free myself from my own complexes and learn to talk about difficult things, but the more I worked with young people, the more I spent time with them, the more workshops I led, the more I understood how important these discussions are.” It’s for them that he takes up these issues in his lyrics.
Les pièces de Raccoon sont empreintes d’: Raccoon’s songs are steeped in honesty, even when they deal with difficult subjects like mental health. He speaks openly about his own experience. “My life hasn’t always been easy. My family and I have had our ups and downs, including <l1>an armed assault</l1>. There were times I sank into depression, like many others,” Raccoon confides. “It’s not true that only white people suffer from mental health problems,” he adds forcefully. “A lot of people I knew were suffering from psychological disorders without me knowing it at the time. Some of them were active in the street and suffered from depression, even the beginnings of schizophrenia.”
Raccoon a une vision claire de son trava: Raccoon has a clear vision of his work. “I talk about my own struggles to help young Black people talk about theirs too. I want to normalize these conversations as much as possible, to break the taboo around mental health in our community.” The artist encourages others to open up and ask for help, because keeping everything inside can only lead to distress.
« Tu peux être beau gosse, talentueux et: “You can be good-looking, talented and sometimes want to die; that’s normal,” he says with conviction. “But don’t keep it to yourself. Talk to a patnè, see a professional, don’t let those toxic thoughts overwhelm you. Because when you keep everything inside, that’s when it starts to grow and become dangerous.”

Shamyr Daléus-Louis qui contemple son po: Shamyr Daléus-Louis contemplating his portrait as Raccoon. Photo: Ahmed El Moudden
Pour conclure, le rappeur remet son chap: To close, the rapper puts his youth worker hat back on to pass an inspiring message on to Montréal’s youth: “DO YOU!” he says passionately. He encourages young people not to follow the crowd, but to follow their own path, whatever that may be. “If you like doing ballet, do ballet!” he insists.
« Le plus beau cadeau que l’homme noir o: “The most beautiful gift a Black man or a Black woman can give themselves is independence of mind. It’s very hard in a predominantly white Western world, where power belongs to them,” Shamyr acknowledges. “Your experience as an individual matters, because I know that when a white person wakes up, they don’t think about how other white people will perceive them.”
« Si vous voulez rapper, rappez ! L’enre: “If you want to rap, rap! Recording in a studio is just the final step… When I was young, I took slam and poetry writing workshops.” By leading rap writing workshops, he gives back to young people in the neighbourhoods. “I want to make the fundamentals of rap accessible to others, the way they were for me… I want to recreate the moments I lived when I was younger, when I went to my writing classes. I’m trying to give them the writing bug again and, thank God, it still works,” he says with a smile.
